title: 2 Chronicles 1:14–17
context: The unit reports Solomon’s chariots, horses, and the abundance of precious metal and cedar in Jerusalem, a notice that stands at the opening of his reign in this book and later, after the queen of Sheba’s visit, in 1 Kings 10:26–29. The two passages should be named as parallels and not forced into one wording. Both record one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen, kept in the chariot cities and with the king at Jerusalem. This chapter says the king made “silver and gold to be as common as stones in Jerusalem”; 1 Kings 10:27 speaks of silver as common as stones and does not add gold in the same clause. Both traditions read the unit as a report of royal wealth and trade, consistent with the already drafted Kings notes, without inventing a party contrast over the wording or over the source of the horses.

verses.text: Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen. He had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen that he placed in the chariot cities, and with the king at Jerusalem.
verses.arminianNotes:
“Solomon gathered chariots and horsemen. He had one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen that he placed in the chariot cities, and with the king at Jerusalem.” The numbers match 1 Kings 10:26, which also reports one thousand four hundred chariots and twelve thousand horsemen kept in the chariot cities and with the king. The Chronicler places the notice here, early in the reign, rather than after the visit of the queen of Sheba.

Arminian readers take the figures as a real report of military and court provision, not as a symbol to be decoded.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the parallel and the different placement. The same counts appear in both books; this chapter does not wait for the later scene in 1 Kings 10.

Both traditions name the agreement and leave the placement difference unforced, without a party contrast over the numbers.

verses.text: The king made silver and gold to be as common as stones in Jerusalem, and he made cedars to be as common as the sycamore trees that are in the lowland.
verses.arminianNotes:
The king made “silver and gold to be as common as stones in Jerusalem, and he made cedars to be as common as the sycamore trees that are in the lowland.” 1 Kings 10:27 says the king made silver as common as stones, and cedars as common as the sycamores in the lowland, and does not add gold in that sentence. The added word should be reported, not explained away.

Arminian readers hear a description of unusual plenty in Jerusalem, gold named here alongside silver, without turning the comparison into allegory.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers likewise set the two sentences side by side. The cedars and the sycamores of the lowland are shared; gold is named in this verse and not in the matching clause of 1 Kings 10:27.

Both traditions read the verse as a report of wealth, consistent with the already drafted 1 Kings 10 notes, and invent no contrast over the extra word.

verses.text: The horses which Solomon had were brought out of Egypt and from Kue. The king’s merchants purchased them from Kue.
verses.arminianNotes:
“The horses which Solomon had were brought out of Egypt and from Kue. The king’s merchants purchased them from Kue.” 1 Kings 10:28 begins with horses brought out of Egypt, then says the merchants “received them in droves”. This verse names Kue twice as a source and a place of purchase. The already drafted 1 Kings 10 notes treat the difference as a question of wording, not as a matter either tradition must settle.

Arminian readers keep both reports in view and refuse to rewrite one line from the other.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also name Kue here and droves in 1 Kings 10:28, without declaring a single reconstructed trade route as if the verse had supplied it.

Both traditions stay consistent with those Kings notes: the source language differs, and the difference is not a theological fork.

verses.text: They imported from Egypt then exported a chariot for six hundred pieces of silver and a horse for one hundred fifty. They also exported them to the Hittite kings and the Syrian kings.
verses.arminianNotes:
They imported from Egypt and then exported “a chariot for six hundred pieces of silver and a horse for one hundred fifty.” The same trade reaches “the Hittite kings and the Syrian kings.” 1 Kings 10:29 gives “six hundred shekels of silver” and “one hundred fifty shekels”, and export to the kings of the Hittites and of Syria. The price is the same scale; the wording for the unit of silver is not identical, and should be left as it stands.

Arminian readers take the trade as a historical report, horses and chariots moving at a stated price, without a moral contrast invented for this verse alone.
verses.reformedNotes:
Reformed readers also keep the two price notices side by side. Pieces of silver here, shekels in 1 Kings 10:29, and the same destinations under slightly different names.

Both traditions close the chapter as a wealth-and-trade notice, in line with the drafted 1 Kings 10 notes, and do not press a party argument about the horses from Egypt.
